name: Ascorbyl glucoside

card.summary: A stabilised vitamin C derivative used in brightening and anti-ageing skincare, with a small evidence base specific to the ingredient itself.
card.note: Efficacy data for this specific derivative are sparse; most vitamin C evidence concerns other forms.

quick.overview:
Ascorbyl glucoside is vitamin C (ascorbic acid) with a glucose unit attached, a modification made to make the molecule more stable in skincare formulas. It appears in serums and creams marketed for brightening, evening skin tone and general anti-ageing.

Published human data specific to it are limited. A small case series used an ascorbyl glucoside preparation together with iontophoresis in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it is listed among whitening ingredients in cosmetic analysis papers.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a precursor that releases ascorbic acid in the skin. Wikipedia notes that the rate at which it converts to ascorbic acid is unknown, and that it is credited with better stability and penetration than ascorbyl phosphate salts.
quick.risks: No specific safety problems are described in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and like other topical products it can be tolerated differently by different people.

lead: Ascorbyl glucoside (also written AA-2G; chemical name L-ascorbic acid 2-O-alpha-glucoside) is a derivative of ascorbic acid in which a glucose unit is attached to the vitamin C molecule. It is commonly used in cosmetic products as a way of delivering vitamin C to the skin [1].

In skincare it is marketed for brightening, evening skin tone and reducing the look of pigmentation, and it appears in cosmetic analytical studies alongside other whitening ingredients such as kojic acid and niacinamide [2][3]. Skincare communities discuss it as a gentler or more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid.

Evidence specific to ascorbyl glucoside is limited. One small uncontrolled study in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation used a proprietary ascorbyl glucoside preparation combined with a device and acid regimen, which makes it hard to attribute any effect to the ingredient alone [4]. Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy data for its use in skin whitening are not given in its source material, and that its rate of conversion to ascorbic acid in the body is unknown [1].

paras: Ascorbyl glucoside is an ascorbic acid derivative containing a glycosyl group; related ascorbyl glucosides have also shown antiscorbutic (anti-scurvy) activity [1]. The molecular formula is C12H18O11 and it is produced through reactions catalysed by glycosyltransferase-class enzymes [1].

Glycosylated forms of ascorbic acid are described in the nutrition literature as products of in vitro transglycosidation rather than compounds found in nature, unlike glycosides of several other vitamins [5].

Plain ascorbic acid is described as a powerful antioxidant with potential skin benefits, but its topical use is limited by instability in conventional formulations [6]. Derivatives such as ascorbyl glucoside are used as an alternative form; Wikipedia says it has been credited with superior stability and penetration compared with ascorbyl phosphate salts [1].
Analytical chemistry papers have developed methods for measuring ascorbyl glucoside in skin-whitening and bleaching cosmetics, indicating its presence in commercial lightening products [2][3][7].

A 2013 study in 35 patients (34 women, 1 man) with melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation used a full-face iontophoresis mask with a proprietary vitamin C (ascorbyl glucoside) preparation, alongside a mandelic/malic acid regimen [4]. It was a combined-treatment study without a comparison group on the ingredient alone.
A 2024 Bayesian network meta-analysis compared 14 molecules for inhibiting UV daylight-induced pigmentation; it addresses topical depigmenting agents as a class [8].
No randomised controlled trial testing ascorbyl glucoside alone against placebo for appearance outcomes was identified.
The sources reviewed do not describe specific adverse-effect findings for ascorbyl glucoside. Regulatory status is not discussed in them.
